articles.title: The Houthis aren't somebody else's problem. America can't afford to look away
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces have expelled Houthis from key areas near the Bab el-Mandeb, but the case for limited U.S. air support grows stronger.
articles.body: Some in Washington would like to believe the Houthis are somebody else’s problem. It is easy to understand why. America is already deeply engaged in the war with Iran, and there is little appetite for widening the battlefield with the midterm elections approaching. The Houthis have also cynically given Washington a reason to limit its involvement by signaling that American shipping will not be targeted. But Yemen is not a separate conflict. The Houthis — a U.S.-designated foreign terrorist organization aligned with Iran and armed and supported by Tehran — are waging a campaign against Yemen’s Saudi-backed government that forms part of the same regional confrontation. The good news is that the war is beginning to move in the right direction for the Yemeni government, although the battle will be challenging and, like all battles, will have its ups and downs. Government forces, supported by Saudi air power, have expelled the Houthis from some strategically important areas around the Bab el-Mandeb and are demonstrating their capacity to operate effectively. These gains remain vulnerable, but the battlefield momentum is encouraging. SAUDI ARABIA TELLS TRUMP NOW IS THE TIME FOR MILITARY ACTION AS IRAN-BACKED HOUTHIS ADVANCE It also changes the calculation of American involvement. The United States is already providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support while stopping short of direct strikes. That assistance is valuable. American satellites and other surveillance systems can help locate missile batteries, drone facilities, command centers and mobile launchers. The case for American support should not rest on the claim that Saudi Arabia and Yemen cannot succeed without it. It should rest on the fact that the United States has a clear interest in helping them succeed. Direct American air power could make that intelligence considerably more effective. U.S. aircraft can operate directly within American intelligence, surveillance and targeting networks, allowing information gathered by satellites and other sensors to move rapidly through the sensor-to-shooter chain. Saudi aircraft can also receive sophisticated U.S. and allied targeting information, including through interoperable systems, but intelligence shared with a partner may require additional dissemination, release and command steps before reaching the aircraft assigned to strike. Even a short delay matters when a mobile missile launcher can fire, relocate and disappear within minutes. Placing American aircraft directly inside this sensor-to-shooter loop could therefore shorten the time between detecting and attacking a target. A limited American role could concentrate on mobile missile launchers, drone facilities and other time-sensitive assets rather than expand into a large or open-ended campaign. It would allow intelligence Washington is already collecting and sharing to be exploited with greater speed and effect. Direct U.S. Air Force involvement would therefore be very helpful, but it is not critical to the campaign’s success. Saudi Arabia has the aircraft, intelligence capabilities and resources necessary to support the Yemeni government, while Yemeni troops are proving capable of conducting the ground fighting themselves. Washington, however, could make the campaign faster and more effective without assuming responsibility for the war. IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR US POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY This distinction matters. The case for American support should not rest on the claim that Saudi Arabia and Yemen cannot succeed without it. It should rest on the fact that the United States has a clear interest in helping them succeed. Geography makes Yemen difficult to ignore. The Houthis have strengthened their position along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. Their ability to threaten Saudi shipping has consequences far beyond Yemen. Roughly 22% of global seaborne container trade passes through the Red Sea. When the route is disrupted, ships must travel around Africa, lengthening journeys and raising freight and insurance costs. HOUTHIS ENTER US 'KILL BOX' AFTER SEIZING RED SEA 'CORK,' FORMER PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS There is also another worrying development. The Houthis are building ties with al-Shabaab in Somalia, al Qaeda’s wealthy East African affiliate. American officials have warned of weapons transfers, training in drones and explosives, and tactical coordination between the groups. This raises the prospect of a militant network operating on both sides of the Gulf of Aden. Its targets may be Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government today, but there is no reason to assume that its priorities will remain unchanged. Energy security makes the issue even more consequential. Saudi Arabia exports oil through the Strait of Hormuz, but its East-West Pipeline also carries crude across the kingdom to Yanbu on the Red Sea. The pipeline provides an alternative route when Hormuz becomes dangerous. Its strategic value declines sharply if the Houthis can threaten the Red Sea simultaneously. OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES Iran and its allies could therefore apply pressure at two critical choke points: Tehran around Hormuz and the Houthis around the Bab el-Mandeb. This is not merely a Saudi or Yemeni problem. China depends heavily on Gulf energy flows, Europe relies on the Red Sea and Suez trading system, and American energy production does not insulate American consumers from global oil prices. The current fighting also exposes the magnitude of the mistake made at Hodeidah in 2018. Saudi- and Emirati-backed Yemeni forces had advanced to the outskirts of the city and placed the Houthis’ principal Red Sea port under severe pressure. Western governments feared that fighting around the port would interrupt supplies of food, fuel and medicine. Those concerns were legitimate, but the solution imposed was strategically disastrous. SAUDI FOREIGN MINISTER WARNS HOUTHI THREAT GOES GLOBAL AS TRUMP HOLDS FIRE Under intense Western pressure, the offensive was stopped. The Stockholm Agreement froze the fighting and called for forces to redeploy from Hodeidah. That withdrawal never occurred as intended. The Houthis retained the port, preserved their economic and military lifeline and used the following years to consolidate their rule, strengthen their relationship with Iran and acquire increasingly sophisticated missiles and drones. articles.title: Kai Cenat’s charity reported $1 million in contributions in 2024; one year later, it held $1.6 million in net assets while planning a school for Nigerian children
articles.summary: Kai Cenat's charitable work in Nigeria has moved from a highly publicised pledge to a project backed by a formal nonprofit and growing financial reserves.
articles.body: Kai Cenat's charitable work in Nigeria has moved from a highly publicised pledge to a project backed by a formal nonprofit and growing financial reserves. The Kai Cenat Foundation reported more than $1 million in contributions in its first reported year, according to its 2024 tax filing. A year later, the foundation reported $1.6 million in net assets while spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on its programme work, including steps toward developing educational facilities in Nigeria. The numbers offer a clearer picture of where the charity stood financially as Cenat continued working on his long-promised school project.Kai Cenat Foundation reported $1 million in contributions in 2024The Kai Cenat Foundation was formed in 2024 as a 501(c)(3) public charity based in Marietta, Georgia. Its stated mission centres on improving access to education in Nigeria through the construction of sustainable educational facilities.Its first Form 990 gives an unusually straightforward picture of the organisation's opening year. The foundation reported $1,001,374 in contributions, gifts and grants during fiscal year 2024. It also reported no functional expenses for that period, leaving the organisation with $1,001,374 in net assets at year-end. The filing shows the money held by the foundation was essentially cash, with no reported liabilities.That does not mean the foundation had already built a school or completed major construction during 2024. Instead, the filing shows that the organisation was still at an early stage of turning its fundraising into a long-term education project.The foundation's programme description said it had begun taking contributions for the school and had contracted SESO Global to begin scouting land. That detail matters because it places the 2024 funds in the context of planning rather than suggesting that the entire amount had already been spent on construction.The filing also lists Cenat as the foundation's president. His compensation was reported as $0 for the year, alongside $0 reported for vice president John Nelson and treasurer Erica Heyward.The charity reached $1.6 million in net assets a year laterThe foundation's next filing shows a notable change.For fiscal year 2025, the Kai Cenat Foundation reported $858,000 in revenue and $233,000 in expenses. More importantly, its net assets had grown to approximately $1.6 million. The exact total assets reported were $1,626,366, while liabilities were listed at zero.The figures show that the foundation did not simply spend through the money it had accumulated during its first year. It continued to hold a substantial reserve while beginning to record programme spending.Its 2025 filing says the organisation contracted with SESO Global and Enko Foundation to begin a feasibility study. The purpose was to understand the needs of the region and determine the best way to provide educational facilities. The foundation also reported providing school supplies and computers to students.The foundation spent $233,000 on programme services during the year, according to the filing. That means the financial story is more complicated than simply looking at the amount raised. Some of the foundation's money remained on its balance sheet while work moved forward on the education initiative.For readers following the project, that distinction is important. Net assets are not the same thing as money already spent on a school. They represent what the nonprofit had left after accounting for its liabilities at the end of the reporting period.Kai Cenat’s Nigerian school project faced delaysThe financial filings also provide context for why the school has taken time to develop.Cenat first drew widespread attention to the project after visiting Nigeria and seeing the conditions at a school in Makoko, a waterfront community in Lagos. He later pledged to help build a new school for children in the area.During Mafiathon 3 in 2025, Cenat provided a more detailed update on the project. The proposed school was initially connected to Makoko, but construction difficulties involving the location forced the team to reconsider the site. Reports later said the project was being moved to Yaba, Lagos, where construction would be more practical.The change in location did not mean that the original community was being abandoned. Reports said children from Makoko would still be able to receive free education once the school opens.The project was also described as a much larger undertaking than simply putting up a building. Land, approvals, construction, curriculum and staffing all have to be considered before a functioning school can open.Cenat acknowledged the long timeline while discussing the project, saying, “it’s impossible to build a new school from the ground up in under two years” if the goal is to create something sustainable. He also described the ambition in simple terms: “Beyond me, beyond streaming.”That statement captures the bigger idea behind the project. Cenat is not presenting the school as a short-term publicity initiative. The stated aim is to create an institution that can continue serving students well beyond his own career as a streamer.What Kai Cenat’s charity finances reveal about the school planThe latest nonprofit figures offer one of the clearest ways to understand the project's progress.The foundation's 2024 filing showed more than $1 million coming in and no reported expenses. By 2025, the organisation had spent $233,000 on programme activity, including work connected to the educational project and direct support such as school supplies and computers. Yet it still ended the year with more than $1.6 million in net assets.That balance gives the foundation room to continue funding planning and development, but it should not be mistaken for the full budget required to complete the school.The wider project has been estimated at $5 million. Cenat also pledged a share of his Mafiathon revenue toward the initiative. During Mafiathon 3, 15% of the revenue was earmarked for the school project, according to Black Enterprise. Cenat's team said the goal was to build a school near Lagos that could provide a lasting educational opportunity for children.The foundation's work has therefore entered a different phase. What began with a pledge is now tied to a registered nonprofit, formal financial reporting, feasibility work and partnerships focused on determining how the school should operate.Cenat also returned to Nigeria in February 2026, renewing attention on the project and its progress. Reports said the visit came after earlier delays involving land acquisition and regulatory issues, with the proposed location shifted from Makoko to Yaba.The school is not yet the finished product that Cenat originally envisioned. But the foundation's financial records show that the effort has continued to develop behind the scenes. With $1.6 million in reported net assets at the end of 2025 and active planning work underway, the focus now is on turning those resources and commitments into a functioning school for Nigerian children.For Cenat, the challenge is no longer simply making a promise. It is delivering a project that can stand on its own, serve students for years and fulfil the larger vision behind his pledge.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: France promises 3,000 extra teachers in bid to calm student protests
articles.summary: Education minister Edouard Geffray makes the offer after another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.
articles.body:
The French government has made its first sign of giving ground to teenage protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Education minister Edouard Geffray made the offer in a television interview on Thursday evening, at the end of another day of sometimes violent demonstrations by high-school students.

The government says 6,877 people have been arrested, 86% of whom are under the age of 18, since protests began centred around demands for more resources in secondary education.

In what unions have billed as Act Four of the three-week movement, some 71,000 people staged protests across the country on Thursday, with 24,000 gathering at the Bastille in Paris.

Police once again intervened with tear-gas to disperse groups who attacked them with paving stones and homemade fireworks.

In Bordeaux, a lycée, or high school, was ransacked by protesters, and in Marseille a deputy-head was beaten up.

On Friday, some 140 lycées - out of 3,500 - were totally or partially closed, a big drop on previous days. But another day of action has been called for next Tuesday.

France's school protests: What lies behind the anger

Geffray's announcement was the first material concession to the protesters' complaints.

It has long been recognised by all concerned in French education that too many school hours are being lost because of absent teachers and their non-replacement by available supply staff.

The minister said that thanks to new software coming online at the ministry, it would be possible to direct 3,000 supply teachers to the 500 or so lycées identified as being in the greatest need.

Many of these schools are likely to be in high-immigration city suburbs, where the lack of teachers is most acute.

Geffray also said that more money would be made available under an already existing scheme for those teachers who want to work overtime hours in order to plug gaps.

And he promised that students' grievances would be taken into account in forthcoming discussions on the education section of the 2027 state budget.

But the offer contained no major promise of new investment on a scale likely to appease protesters.

The government is wary of appearing to buy social peace because it knows France's precarious debt situation is being followed closely by international money markets.

Reaction from student leaders has been guarded to say the least.

Nathanaël Combary, who represents the most moderate of the three main lycée unions Renouveau Lycéen (Lycée Renewal), said students were waiting to see how the promise was carried out in practice: "We've had some announcements which correspond to part of our demands. But obviously people want to see the money and more concrete results."

"As long as we do not have €10bn on the table, we will continue our action," said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Etudiante (Student Union), which is close to the radical-left France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party of presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Mélenchon praised Thursday's demonstrations, saying on X that the students had "retaken the Bastille".

But at the other end of the political spectrum, a spokesman for the hard-right National Rally (RN) condemned the government's concessions.

"The message is: if you break things, you get given stuff," said Laurent Jacobelli. "When you burn cars, attack police, you gain something in return. It's the legitimisation of violence."

The movement is the most serious student unrest in France in many years, and comes against a backdrop of rising tension in the country - with anger over rising fuel prices and distress in the farming sector also liable to trigger protests.

Next Saturday, 17 October, has been earmarked as a day of demonstrations by a revived "yellow vest" movement, which forced the government to halt a rise in fuel taxes after protests and riots in 2018.

In addition, the approach of presidential elections in April and May - in which both hard right and hard left are expected to perform strongly - is exacerbating the mood of confrontation.

The government is hoping that the approach of half-term holidays at the end of next week - as well as the arrival of colder and wetter weather - will take some of the sting out of the protests.

articles.title: Doctor accused of 1994 Rwanda genocide offences to face trial in UK
articles.summary: Dr Vincent Brown was allegedly a "leader" or "supervisor" of violent acts carried out by others in the early days of the genocide.
articles.body:
A doctor accused of a number of offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide is set to face trial in autumn next year.

Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group in Rwanda. He is the first person in the UK to have been charged over the genocide.

Brown, of Islington, north London, is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.

A judge has now set his provisional trial date to begin in October 2027. He denies wrongdoing and has not yet entered a plea.

The defendant appeared via video link from Belmarsh prison on Friday for a pre-trial hearing at the Old Bailey during which Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb set a provisional eight to 12-week trial from October 4 2027.

A plea and case management hearing has also been set for 15 January.

He has indicated he will plead not guilty to the charges against him.

An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were killed during the 1994 Rwanda genocide which lasted for 100 days .

Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.

Between April 6 and 13 1994, he was allegedly a party to six murders and was later charged following a seven-year British investigation into the killings.

The court heard on Friday that a £100,000 bail condition , imposed earlier in October, had not yet been met.

Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC told the court the events in 1994 were "the most devastating wave of mass killing in modern history".

Jones said: "One hundred thousand were murdered in Kigali especially in the first days and weeks of the genocide."

articles.title: Birmingham Airport expansion plan 'a huge vote of confidence'
articles.summary: The airport has unveiled a £2bn plan which could more than double passenger numbers to 30 million.
articles.body:
Plans to expand Birmingham Airport have prompted a mixed reaction from residents and business leaders.

The airport has unveiled a £2bn plan which could more than double passenger numbers to 30 million and create more than 50,000 jobs, 3,800 of them on site.

While some people who live under flight paths near the airport have questioned the impact of future growth on local communities, business groups have welcomed the plans as a boost for the West Midlands.

Raj Kandola, deputy chief executive of the Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce, told BBC Radio WM the plans were a "massive vote of confidence" for the region.

An eight-week public consultation will be held over the plans and chief executive Nick Barton said the scheme would aim to ensure the airport was "ready for the future" but needed a "fair and stable taxation environment".

Birmingham Airport announces £2bn expansion

The hunt for a new generation of blood donors

However, some families in the area are worried about how the proposed expansion will affect their quality of life.

Nicki Sweet, from Aldridge, said aircraft noise could be "constant" on some days.

"It can be quite intense. You can have one after another, all throughout the night," she said.

Sweet also questioned whether the airport should deal with existing issues before expanding further.

"Using the airport myself, we know there are issues with delays, getting through security, cancellations and baggage," she said.

"Maybe they need to sort them first without proceeding."

Hundreds of passengers were affected by issues with the airport's baggage system in August, with left many without their luggage.

Audrey Hurdman, from Erdington, said aircraft noise had become more noticeable in recent years despite living some distance from the airport.

"I've lived here for 50 years. It's never been this bad," she said.

"The jobs are a good thing, but are there going to be more planes late at night?"

West Bromwich resident Nigel Fearn uses the airport once a year and said the prospect of new jobs was welcome, but questioned whether the extra flights were needed, particularly with the impact of the extra emissions.

Not all residents are against the plans.

Leanne Bryan, vice chair of the Tile Cross residents neighbourhood forum, said she had lived on the flight patch for more than 35 years.

"I love living where I do," she said, adding that the airport cannot move, but "residents can".

"If they don't like it don't move there."

Balancing concerns about extra flights is the likely scale of investment and the number of jobs tied to it.

Kandola, said the ambition of the project was "something to behold".

"If you're getting more tourists into the region, more business and more investment, that can only be a good thing," he said.

Richard Parker, the Labour mayor of the West Midlands, also welcomed the "ambitious masterplan" which he said would improve international links and unlock vital backing for local businesses and supply chains.

Airport chiefs said the "unprecedented" proposals set out a "clear commitment" to continue serving the region.

They added they wanted to make sure the growth was "delivered responsibly and sustainably" for the people living near the site.

The first stage of development could start in 2027, with investment in areas such as baggage and terminal facilities, additional aircraft stands and accessibility.

People can give feedback on the plans online, by post or attend any of the 20 events, which start in Hampton in Arden on 16 October.

articles.summary: A classics professor weighed in on a 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck off Turkey that yielded luxury ceramics linked to Cicero, with ancient coins helping researchers date the find.
articles.body: A 2,100-year-old shipwreck off the coast of Turkey has revealed thousands of luxury dishes of a type once prized by Cicero, the famed Roman statesman whose writings later influenced America's Founding Fathers — with an expert calling the find "quite rare." The recovery was recently announced by Turkish officials, the state-run Anadolu Agency (AA) reported Sept. 28. Pictures show divers working among piles of ancient pottery, with ceramic plates and bowls scattered across the sandy seabed. ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS SAYINGS ABOUT ROME MAY BE WRONG, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS The artifacts include 122 different forms and sizes of plates, bowls and trays, including dishes used for nuts, soup and fish. Researchers believe the ship was traveling from Rhosus to Rome when it struck a shallow area during a storm and sank, according to AA. The wreck lies about 138 to 180 feet below the surface. The discovery is particularly significant because the ceramics are believed to have originated in Rhosus, a production center mentioned in the writings of Cicero — though there's no evidence that the recovered dishes belonged to Cicero himself. Cicero, one of ancient Rome's most celebrated orators and politicians, significantly influenced the U.S.' Founding Fathers, especially Thomas Jefferson and John Adams. DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS In a letter to his friend Atticus in 50 B.C., the statesman wrote that he had ordered ceramic vessels from Rhosus for him, according to AA. Taco Terpstra, a professor of classics and history at Northwestern University, told Fox News Digital that the discovery offers an unusual opportunity to connect ancient artifacts with historical writings. "It's unusual that we have so much of this type of ceramic," Terpstra said. DAMAGED FRAGMENT DEEMED 'UNREMARKABLE' TURNS OUT TO BE RARE PIECE OF HOMER'S 'ODYSSEY' HISTORY He explained that coins found aboard the ship help researchers date the wreck, while the pottery can be traced to a production region in what is now southern Turkey and northern Syria. articles.title: Ex-first minister Mark Drakeford suggests Wales Office should go
articles.summary: Created 60 years ago, most of the powers it used to hold were transferred to Cardiff Bay in 1999.
articles.body:
Former Labour First Minister Mark Drakeford has said it is time to consider scrapping the UK government's Wales Office.

Drakeford said "the time has come" to think about abolishing the department, which was largely stripped of its powers when devolution began in 1999.

Asked on S4C's Y Byd yn ei Le if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that."

But Labour MP Ruth Jones described the suggestion as "foolish", arguing Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock was "fighting the corner for Wales".

The future of the Wales Office has been the subject of regular speculation since devolution, with successive UK governments considering whether its functions could be folded into a single department, also covering Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Earlier this year, then-First Minister Eluned Morgan said there remained " a role " for the Welsh secretary, but argued the post should be "the voice of Wales at the cabinet table" rather than "the UK government's voice in Wales".

Under a previous UK Labour government, Peter Hain combined cabinet responsibility for Wales and Northern Ireland between 2005 and 2007.

Asked if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that.

"Of course, [former Labour prime minister] Tony Blair thought of this too.

"This has been part of discussions in Westminster not only now but for more than a decade."

The post of Welsh secretary, or secretary of state for Wales, was created by Harold Wilson's Labour government in October 1964, with the Welsh Office opening the following April.

In 1999 the Welsh Office's powers over areas including health, education, environment, agriculture and transport were taken over by the Welsh Assembly, now known as the Senedd , and what remained of the UK government department was given the title of Wales Office.

Interviewed on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday , Ruth Jones dismissed the idea of abolishing it.

"I've got tremendous respect for Mark Drakeford but, let's be honest, he's now retired and, therefore, let the politicians who are elected to get on with the job get on with the job," she said.

"In terms of the Wales Office, the only person from Wales actually at the [UK] cabinet table is the secretary of state for Wales, and he is there fighting the corner for Wales.

"So I would say to disband that would be foolish."

Staffordshire Police has launched an AI-powered chatbot to answer non-emergency queries from people, in a bid to cut waiting times and free up call handlers for more complex cases.

The force claimed it was the first in the West Midlands to introduce Bobbi, an AI-virtual assistant, available through the live chat function on its website.

Ch Supt Matthew Morgan, head of the force's contact centre, said one of the most common questions from the public was whether an incident was a crime.

Bobbi is designed to provide answers to routine inquiries, alongside existing online forms, telephone lines and front counters.

"It's designed to make it as easy and as fast as possible to get people answers to common questions," Morgan added.

The force said the chatbot had undergone "robust and relentless challenges" before being launched for a 12-month trial period.

"We wouldn't have deployed it otherwise," Morgan said.

The technology has already been trialled by a number of other forces, including Merseyside Police , Thames Valley Police and Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary.

Staffordshire Police said Bobbi would not replace human call handlers, but help reduce demand on the contact centre.

"Ultimately, what it does is free up our call handlers to focus on those complex and urgent inquiries that absolutely 100% necessitate a human agent," Ch Supt Morgan said.

Bobbi cannot be used to report crimes and is not replacing the 999 emergency service, the force said. Complex or sensitive inquiries will also continue to be dealt with by human staff.

articles.title: CJP protest on October 10: SC's order on Delhi restrictions explained in 10 points
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday pushed back against sweeping transport restrictions in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest,
articles.body: The Supreme Court on Friday pushed back against sweeping transport restrictions in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest, observing that security measures should not bring the city’s public transport network to a standstill.The bench cautioned that an entire city cannot be shut down in the name of managing a protest, warning that blanket curbs on metro and train services could cause severe hardship to ordinary citizens.READ ALSO: 'Anti-monopoly, not anti-business': Rahul Gandhi demands 'level playing field' for corporationsA bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, was hearing petitions challenging the proposed closure of 57 metro stations and the cancellation of long-distance trains to the capital.Here are 10 key takeaways from the proceedings and the court’s directions:1. No complete shutdown of metro servicesThe court made clear that metro trains cannot be completely stopped. “There shall be no complete prohibition on the movement of metro trains,” it said in its order.2. Authorities must reconsider restrictionsSolicitor general Tushar Mehta told the bench he would urge the authorities to allow metro and other railway services to operate in a suitably regulated manner.3. Public convenience must be protectedThe bench highlighted the impact on students, employees, senior citizens and other commuters who rely on public transport to reach Delhi from neighbouring areas. "Exercise caution. Exercise an abundance of caution. There is nothing wrong with that. You are responsible for maintaining law and order. But that responsibility is not merely about protecting State property", it said.4. Security measures must be proportionateChief Justice Surya Kant said authorities could restrict unruly movement but should not deprive ordinary citizens of transport facilities.5. Court invokes proportionality"One very important principle that we follow for every citizen is the principle of proportionality. You have to prevent certain things. Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," the CJI said.6. Train cancellations raised in courtSenior advocate Kapil Sibal flagged the cancellation of long-distance trains, arguing that passengers scheduled to arrive during the notified period would be unable to reach Delhi.7. Road restrictions also need reviewThe bench said authorities should examine which areas required regulation and which did not, stressing that “there should be a free flow of traffic”.8. Traffic advisory orderedThe court directed Delhi authorities to issue a traffic advisory for people travelling within the city by road.9. Revised decisions must be publicisedAuthorities were directed to give wide publicity to decisions on regulated metro and railway operations to minimise further inconvenience to commuters.10. Centre asked to consider an alternative protest venueThe court asked the Union government to consider identifying a suitable location with adequate facilities for peaceful and lawful protests.The CJP protest is scheduled for October 10 at Jantar Mantar, with organisers demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral roll irregularities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
articles.summary: The prime minister says restrictions on what workers can do after leaving roles have "gone too far".
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico and The Financial Times , alongside the Budget on 28 October.

Responding to the prime minister's comments, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes to non-compete rules, adding they played a "vital role" in protecting commercially sensitive information and client relationships.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

articles.title: An anonymous donor gave $1 million to help Pennsylvania nurses pay student loans amid mounting debt; the gift inspired others to give $3 million more
articles.summary: An anonymous donor gave $1 million to help nurses repay student loans at Lankenau Medical Center in Wynnewood, Pennsylvania, after recognising the care
articles.body: An anonymous donor gave $1 million to help nurses repay student loans at Lankenau Medical Center in Wynnewood, Pennsylvania, after recognising the care they provided during several hospital stays. The donation offered financial relief to nurses facing education debt alongside family responsibilities and other expenses. In the first round of assistance, all 179 nurses who applied received grants of up to $3,600. The initiative later extended beyond Lankenau Medical Center, with donations supporting nurses at three other hospitals in the Main Line Health system. By March 2026, the four hospitals had received donations totalling $4.26 million, helping 706 nurses with student loan costs.The student loan struggles behind a $1 million donation to nursesEmmy McManus, a registered nurse who had worked at Lankenau Medical Center for 30 years, struggled to repay her student loans while dealing with serious illnesses in her family. After earning her nursing degree, she faced mounting expenses as her parents required medical care, special meals and eventually hospice services. The financial pressure made it difficult to manage her education debt alongside her family responsibilities. The grant funded by the anonymous donor helped ease that burden. Another nurse who received assistance, emergency room nurse Samantha Baldwin-Arroyo, was also managing student loan repayments while caring for her mother, who had chronic illnesses. Baldwin-Arroyo had previously undergone cancer treatment herself. The grant helped cover payments on one of her student loans.Why an anonymous donor gave $1 million to Pennsylvania nursesThe original donation came from a longtime patient who was grateful for the nursing care received during several hospital stays. The donor wanted to recognise the staff members who had helped during those experiences and direct the money towards their financial needs. Rather than funding hospital equipment or a new medical programme, the gift was designed to help nurses repay education loans. Lankenau Medical Center president Katie Galbraith described the idea as “caring for the caregivers”. The donation was announced in October 2024, and the first round of grants subsequently provided financial assistance to 179 nurses who applied, with each eligible recipient receiving up to $3,600.How the donation inspired another $1 million giftThe story attracted wider attention after The Philadelphia Inquirer reported on the Lankenau donation in June 2025. The coverage inspired another anonymous donor to contribute $1 million to Paoli Hospital, also part of Main Line Health, to help its nurses with student loan debt. Among the nurses who benefited was Damacia Gilbert, a single mother who had been taking extra shifts to manage her expenses while paying student loans and covering preschool costs for her son. The grant offered relief from those competing financial pressures. The Paoli donation demonstrated how the original gift had encouraged another donor to support nurses facing similar challenges.Three more hospitals received donations for nurse student loansThe initiative expanded as additional anonymous donors contributed to student loan relief at other Main Line Health hospitals. The original donor gave another $1 million to Lankenau after receiving thank-you letters from nurses. Riddle Hospital in Media, Pennsylvania, received a further $260,000, while Bryn Mawr Hospital received a separate $1 million donation. Together, the contributions brought the total across Lankenau, Paoli, Riddle and Bryn Mawr hospitals to $4.26 million by March 2026. The donations supported 706 nurses, with grants of up to $3,600 available to help with education debt.How the grants eased nurses’ financial burdensThe grants were intended to reduce student loan pressure rather than guarantee that every recipient would become debt-free. For some nurses, the assistance covered loan payments; for others, it helped them get closer to clearing their remaining balances. At Bryn Mawr Hospital, emergency room nurse Bianca Abate had around $30,000 in student loans and said the grant gave her some breathing room. Allyson Smyth, a nurse in the hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit, said the assistance came close to covering her remaining debt. The experiences of recipients showed how targeted financial help could make a difference to healthcare workers balancing loan repayments with family responsibilities and everyday living costs.A $1 million donation grew into a $4.26 million initiativeWhat began as one patient’s effort to thank nurses developed into a wider programme of support across four hospitals in southeastern Pennsylvania. The donations did not erase every recipient’s debt, but they offered direct financial assistance to nurses managing education loans alongside the demands of their work and personal lives. By March 2026, the gifts had reached $4.26 million and helped 706 nurses. The initiative also showed how public attention around a donation could encourage other donors to support a specific need within the healthcare workforce.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2016, Dakota Johnson paid $3.55 million for a 1947 Los Angeles midcentury home; after renovating the 'tree house' with Pierce & Ward, she sold it a decade later for $5.92 million after asking $6 million
articles.summary: Dakota Johnson has sold the Los Angeles home she once described as a leafy “tree house” for $5,924,372, bringing the property’s decade-long chapter under
articles.body: Dakota Johnson has sold the Los Angeles home she once described as a leafy “tree house” for $5,924,372, bringing the property’s decade-long chapter under her ownership to a close. The actress paid $3.55 million for the midcentury residence in January 2016, shortly after her career reached a new level through the Fifty Shades of Grey franchise. She later renovated the property with design firm Pierce & Ward and showcased the finished home in an Architectural Digest feature. Realtor.com reported that the three-bedroom, three-bathroom house was listed for $6 million and went under contract within days. Although the final price was slightly below the asking amount, Johnson still secured a significant increase over her original purchase price.A home with Hollywood historyBuilt in 1947, the residence was designed by architect Carl Maston, whose work was influenced by the principles of California modernism. The house occupies just over 3,200 square feet and sits on more than 0.2 acres in a quiet, tree-filled part of Los Angeles, as per the report.Maston was connected to two of the most important names in midcentury architecture, Richard Neutra and John Lautner. Johnson previously told Architectural Digest that Maston, Lautner and Neutra were friends who would meet at Musso & Frank Grill, the historic Hollywood restaurant. Maston eventually married a hostess at the restaurant, and the couple lived in the house.That history added to the property’s appeal when Johnson first viewed it. The actress said it was only the second home she saw while looking for a place to buy, but she immediately responded to its combination of clean architectural lines and comfortable interiors. “I was immediately drawn to how it was clean but also cozy... I thought, ‘I’ll never want to sell this place'," Johnson told Architectural Digest.Her first major purchaseJohnson bought the home at a significant moment in her professional life. She became an international star with her role as Anastasia Steele in the Fifty Shades films, and she purchased this property at that time. For the actress, the house was not simply another piece of real estate. She said having a permanent home was important because her work schedule could change quickly and often required travel. A private base gave her a place where she could return between projects, she shared with Architectural Digest.That sense of stability was reflected in the way she renovated and decorated the property. Rather than turning it into a glossy celebrity showpiece, Johnson worked with Pierce & Ward to make the home feel personal, warm and connected to its original design.Preserving the midcentury characterThe renovation retained several features that defined Maston’s design. Expansive glass walls open towards the swimming pool and backyard, allowing natural light to reach the main living areas. Wood walls, exposed beams and bold red brick give the interior a textured, organic character. The design also maintains the house’s connection with the surrounding landscape. The main living level was arranged so that the boundary between the interior and exterior feels almost invisible. From inside, residents can look directly towards the pool and garden, while outdoor spaces become an extension of the living room.Not every original feature could be saved. Pierce & Ward co-founder Emily Ward explained that the cork flooring on the second level was no longer usable. The designers replaced it with hardwood, choosing a more durable material while preserving the relaxed character of the home.The resulting interiors combine concrete flooring, natural wood and glass. The effect is modern without feeling cold, which may explain why Johnson referred to the house as a sanctuary.A personal and playful interiorJohnson’s personality was visible throughout the home. During the Architectural Digest tour, she displayed personal objects, family keepsakes and artwork collected over the years. Among the items were a note from her grandmother, actor Tippi Hedren, a photograph connected to Johnson’s appearance on Saturday Night Live and works by artists including David Hockney and Harmony Korine.The primary suite received particularly close attention during the renovation. It includes a large bedroom, a spacious walk-in wardrobe and a bathroom finished in a custom pink tone. The colour was inspired by a sweater Johnson owned from The Row, the fashion label founded by Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, as per the report by Realtor.com.. It further shared that a large soaking tub sits in the centre of the bathroom, positioned near a door that opens towards the outdoors. The room also includes double sinks, a feature Johnson jokingly described as an important part of a healthy relationship.These personal touches prevented the property from feeling like a staged architectural exhibit. Although the house had a notable design history, it was clearly adapted for modern living and shaped around the actress’s own routines.Outdoor spaces and the saleThe home’s exterior includes a swimming pool, barbecue area, fire pit and several patios for relaxing and entertaining. One elevated outdoor perch overlooks the yard, while trees and layered landscaping provide privacy around the property.Johnson listed the residence for $6 million through Ruby Fay of Engel & Volkers Beverly Hills. Realtor.com reported that the property went under contract only days after appearing on the market. Records later showed that the final sale price was $5,924,372.Compared with Johnson’s $3.55 million purchase price in 2016, the sale represents an increase of approximately $2.37 million. That figure does not account for renovation costs, property taxes, maintenance, commission and other expenses, but it still reflects the home’s appeal and the strength of its location.The sale also came despite Johnson’s earlier statement that she expected to remain in the house indefinitely. Reports have since linked her to another Los Angeles property in Outpost Estates, a Mediterranean-style residence purchased for approximately $5.3 million.The end of an eraJohnson’s former home was more than a high-value Los Angeles property. It was the place she chose when her career was accelerating and when she wanted a private anchor amid an unpredictable professional life. Over the years, she preserved its midcentury identity while adding the comforts and personal details that made it her own.Now, the 1947 house has passed to a new owner after selling for nearly $6 million. Its leafy setting, architectural history and carefully renovated interiors helped it achieve a price far above Johnson’s original investment. For a home that once represented stability for the actress, the sale marks the closing of a personal chapter and the beginning of another one for the celebrated California residence.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Why can’t she?’: China restaurant owner gifts two employees BMWs worth Rs 43 lakh each after seeing them commute on electric scooters in harsh cold
articles.summary: For many employees, a good performance review might mean a bonus, a salary hike or a promotion.
articles.body: For many employees, a good performance review might mean a bonus, a salary hike or a promotion. But two workers at a restaurant chain in China received a reward few would expect from their employer: brand-new BMW cars, paid for in full by their boss. The unusual gift came from Ma Yanli, who owns a beef hotpot restaurant chain headquartered in Jiaozuo, in central China’s Henan province. According to the *South China Morning Post*, Ma decided to gift the cars after seeing her employees travel to work on electric scooters in harsh weather. The experience made her think about how differently she and her staff travelled to work, eventually inspiring her to do something about it.A cold morning that led to an unexpected decisionMa had reportedly been thinking about her employees’ daily commutes since the previous winter. One morning, she noticed Li Jie, an employee who had worked at the restaurant for eight years, arriving after riding an electric scooter through the cold. Li’s face was flushed, her ears had turned purple and her hands were stiff from the cold wind. Seeing her struggle made Ma compare the employee’s journey with her own comfortable commute in a car.“I said to myself, 'I can sit in my car and enjoy warmth and convenience during transportation.' Why can’t she?” Ma said. That question eventually turned into a plan to help some of her employees travel more comfortably. Rather than simply giving them a cash bonus, Ma decided to buy them cars. On September 24, she took some workers to a BMW showroom. The employees reportedly did not know what awaited them. According to reports, Ma had purchased the vehicles around two weeks earlier and paid the full amount in advance. Each BMW cost 300,000 yuan, or approximately Rs 43 lakh to Rs 43.2 lakh. The cars were gifts, meaning the selected employees did not have to contribute money towards their purchase.Employees stunned by the surpriseLi was one of the two employees who received a car. Even while travelling to the showroom, she had no idea that she was about to become the owner of a BMW. Ma had reportedly described the gift as a “big toy”, leaving Li unaware of the scale of the surprise. “I am so thrilled! I dared not think about this before. On the way to the BMW showroom, Boss Ma just told me she would gift me a big toy,” Li said. The car was registered in Li’s name on the same day. She did not have to pay anything for it, and Ma did not ask her to sign an agreement in exchange for the gift.Another employee, Liu Yingying, received a grey BMW. Her selection was linked to her hard work and performance at the restaurant. “My boss told me you work hard and your performance is excellent. You deserve this car,” Liu said. For both employees, the gifts represented a significant change to their daily commute. What had started as a routine journey to work on electric scooters had led to an unexpected reward worth lakhs of rupees.‘My company’s prosperity’ comes from employees, says MaFor Ma, the cars were about more than recognising individual performance. She said the success of her business depended on the collective effort of the people working for her, and she wanted them to benefit from that success as well. “I have achieved success in my career. But my company’s prosperity is attributed to the collective efforts of all my employees. So I must let my workers also benefit from the success of my company,” she said.Her decision has drawn attention because it went well beyond the bonuses and gifts commonly associated with employee appreciation. Instead of offering a standard workplace reward, Ma chose a gift that addressed a practical difficulty she had witnessed herself. The story has also prompted discussion about what employers can do to recognise their staff. While a luxury car is an extraordinary gift that most workplaces cannot replicate, Ma’s explanation points to a broader idea: employees contribute to a business’s growth, and their well-being matters too. For Li and Liu, that idea came with car keys. For Ma, it was a way of showing that the people helping build her business should also share in its success.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops enter Tigray
articles.summary: Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes.
articles.body:
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.

In a letter sent to the UN Security Council and seen by the BBC, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence".

Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.

Fighting broke out two weeks ago between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.

Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing the TPLF, which it denies.

During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.

But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.

Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.

Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.

US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.

One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.

Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.

There have so far been no verified reports of casualties. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray.

Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."

But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.

On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".

In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".

Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.

This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.

Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

articles.title: 'Nothing can stop India's youth': Chirag Paswan on metro, train curbs ahead of Oct 10 CJP protest
articles.summary: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday said “nothing can stop” India’s youth, as Indian Railways cancelled several Mail and Express trains scheduled to
articles.body: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday said “nothing can stop” India’s youth, as Indian Railways cancelled several Mail and Express trains scheduled to arrive in Delhi ahead of a protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar on October 10 over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls.Union minister and Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) chief Paswan, a BJP ally and NDA member, also said Indian youth could not be held back, questioning attempts to disrupt their movement. “These are the youth of India—nothing can stop them. To those attempting to spread such misconceptions, I ask: how many trains can anyone really stop? How much connectivity can be blocked? How many roads can be jammed?” Paswan said.Paswan has also sought to distinguish his position on the Election Commission of India (ECI) from an automatic defence of the ruling establishment. Amid the controversy, he had initially said being part of the Union government did not mean he would blindly defend anyone. He stressed that the ECI was an independent constitutional body and called on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to present a robust response to the allegations and address public questions to help restore confidence in the poll panel.However, days later, Paswan said he was satisfied with the ECI’s point-by-point clarifications and criticised the Opposition for what he described as “selective criticism”. His remarks marked a shift from calling for the poll panel to address concerns to endorsing its subsequent explanation.According to news agency ANI, Paswan also said on Friday that the Indian youth have the potential to lead the world, “they possess the capacity to show the world the way—just as previous generations have done—and so, nothing can hold them back.”The remarks come as the Railway Board has directed the cancellation at source of Mail and Express trains departing after 2 pm on October 9 and scheduled to reach New Delhi or Hazrat Nizamuddin stations between 4 am and 2 pm on October 10. Sources said the decision followed intelligence inputs and traffic advisories warning of severe congestion around the stations.Also Read| Chirag Paswan's UP gamble: Why PM Modi's 'Hanuman' is flexing his muscle against alliesPaswan acknowledged that protests were a democratic right but argued that repeated demonstrations and road blockades inconvenienced ordinary citizens.“In a democracy like India, there is certainly scope for protests, and you should by all means protest. However, I want to understand this: if your sole objective is merely to protest, then go ahead—do it today, or even ten days from now. But protests alone will not yield a solution; dialogue will,” he told ANI.He alleged that Opposition parties were using the issue for political purposes and called on them to engage constructively with the Election Commission to address concerns over the electoral-roll revision.“If you have genuine concerns, go to the Election Commission; I am fully confident that the CEC himself would sit down to answer your questions,” Paswan said.The CJP protest is seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Delhi Police has denied permission for the proposed gathering, citing short notice, previous non-compliance with directions, and concerns over public safety, law and order and traffic management.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke criticised the railway restrictions, writing on X, “Shut down the entire country if you are scared of the youth.”Trinamool Congress leader Derek O’Brien also targeted the government over the cancellations of the Howrah-New Delhi Rajdhani Express and Sealdah-New Delhi Rajdhani Express.“This is a big win for the youth of India and @Cockroachisback @abhijeet_dipke Bravo! Even before a ball has been bowled, the shit scared government has its knickers in a twist! (sic)” O’Brien posted on X.Meanwhile, Communist Party of India (Marxist) general secretary M A Baby has approached the Supreme Court challenging the restrictions ahead of the protest, including train cancellations and proposed metro station closures. Senior advocate Kapil Sibal is representing him, according to the party.Delhi Police has also urged the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation to shut 57 stations, while security has been tightened at several Delhi borders. articles.title: Trump signs order to ease diesel costs ahead of midterms: Will it bring relief to US farmers and truckers?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is facing rising pressure to bring down fuel prices as increasing costs squeeze American households and businesses ahead of the
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is facing rising pressure to bring down fuel prices as increasing costs squeeze American households and businesses ahead of the November midterm elections.Despite measures to boost diesel supplies and reduce fuel taxes, prices remain elevated, raising questions about how much the administration can do to ease the burden on consumers in the coming weeks.Diesel prices in the US have climbed sharply since the US-Israel war with Iran began in February, with the average price hovering around $6.30 per gallon in early October.The conflicts involving Iran and Russia’s war with Ukraine have disrupted global fuel supplies, pushing up costs for farmers, truckers and other businesses that depend on diesel.According to news agency Reuters, US diesel prices have risen by around 70 per cent since the war with Iran began, even after the Trump administration backed the release of emergency fuel reserves and expanded access to tax-exempt diesel.The surge in fuel prices has also become a political concern for Republicans, who are seeking to defend their narrow congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections. The cost of living remains a major issue for voters, particularly in rural areas that traditionally support the Republican Party.What has Trump done to lower fuel prices?Trump signed an executive order this week to temporarily expand the use of red-dyed diesel on public roads. The fuel, normally reserved for off-road uses such as farming and construction, is exempt from certain fuel taxes.The move is intended to help farmers, truckers and businesses reduce operating costs. Trump has said the measure could save truckers more than $100 each time they fill up, while also lowering costs for farmers and helping reduce the prices of goods and groceries.However, the plan faces practical challenges. Although red-dyed diesel is chemically identical to regular diesel, its tax-exempt status means that its use on public roads is normally restricted.The temporary relaxation of the rules is intended to make the fuel more accessible, but retailers and fuel suppliers have raised concerns over tax liabilities, logistical difficulties and the risk of penalties when vehicles cross state lines.The savings could also be limited when diesel prices remain above $6 per gallon.The administration has also sought to ease supply concerns through an agreement among G7 countries to release 100 million barrels of oil and petroleum products from emergency reserves. Trump had pressed allies to make more fuel available to the market.Several US states have also reduced or suspended certain fuel taxes, providing some relief to consumers and businesses. However, a reduction in federal gasoline taxes would require congressional approval, making it more difficult to implement before the elections.Why are fuel prices still high in the US?The main challenge for the administration is that fuel prices are being driven by global supply disruptions rather than taxes alone.The war involving Iran has disrupted the flow of oil and refined petroleum products through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global energy supplies. Meanwhile, Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have added pressure to the market.Although some oil flows have recovered, prices remain elevated, with the impact extending to diesel and gasoline. Higher energy costs have also contributed to inflation, putting additional pressure on household budgets and businesses.Can Trump bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections?Trump has already used several policy options available to his administration, but analysts say a sustained reduction in fuel prices will depend largely on developments in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine conflict.Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, told the BBC that the president had largely used the smaller measures available to him, while prices remained elevated. A meaningful and lasting reduction would require easing the geopolitical tensions disrupting energy supplies.Even if the conflicts subside, a quick return to normal prices is not guaranteed. Damage to energy infrastructure in the Middle East could take months to repair, delaying a full recovery in production.Higher fuel and grocery bills have become a concern for voters ahead of the November 3 elections, putting pressure on the administration to demonstrate that it can ease the cost of living.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
articles.summary: Deputy party leader Daisy Cooper says "the vast majority of our MPs support Ed... and are furious at this distraction."
articles.body:
Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.

As first reported by the Financial Times , the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.

Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment.

Lib Dem MP and former leader Tim Farron also defended Sir Ed, saying under his leadership the party was in a position to match or even beat the "record numbers of MPs" the party won at the last election.

"To think we're helped by this kind of rubbish, you'd need to be smoking the kind of stuff even we aren't in favour of legalising," he quipped.

Julian Brazil, a Liberal Democrat council leader who has previously been critical of Sir Ed, said Maynard had "put his head above the parapet - we'll see if other people follow".

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live's Matt Chorley, he said: "I would have thought that in the next few days, we will see if there's a groundswell behind him."

Brazil added that Sir Ed had been a "fantastic leader" but added: "For whatever reasons people aren't listening to Ed, they don't take notice of him, so we need to have a fresh start and be able to articulate what our vision of the country is.

"I think that's best done by someone else."

Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000.

Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm.

He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers.

Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons.

Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs.

To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties.

Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats.

However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels.

More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.

Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said.

One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

articles.title: Nationwide cashier to repay £12k after stealing from customers
articles.summary: Kelly Kershaw stole from vulnerable customers to fund a safari in Africa and a trip to Paris.
articles.body:
A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000.

Kelly Kershaw, 54, stole £13,333 including from vulnerable and elderly customers at Nationwide in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, even forging the signature of a man with learning disabilities.

Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud after colleagues spotted Facebook posts of her on safari in Africa, and on trips to Paris, Tuscany and Dubai.

She was jailed for 16 months in May but returned to Caernarfon Crown Court for a Proceeds of Crime Act hearing, and told to pay back £12,630 - the amount of money she had in assets.

Judge Jones ordered Kershaw to repay the sum within three months or face a further five months in prison.

The mother-of-two posted pictures of skiing trips, safaris and romantic European getaways on her Facebook page and boasted she was "living and loving life one adventure at a time".

Kershaw's victims included an 85-year-old man who had lost some "cognitive abilities" after suffering a stroke - and she stole £6,300 from him.

On one occasion, he came to the branch asking to withdraw £200, but Kershaw logged the withdrawal as £500 and pocketed £300 herself.

Another victim was a 49-year-old man with learning difficulties who lost £1,400 to Kershaw - he had his bank card kept in the branch as he was a previous victim of fraud.

During the May hearing, prosecutor Elen Owen said Kershaw had been transferred to work at the branch in June 2020, which had a "high number of vulnerable customers".

"After a while co-workers noticed the defendant appeared to have a lavish lifestyle," she said.

"She was regularly going on expensive foreign holidays and there were other indications of extravagant spending."

Owen said "due to the suspicions raised" an internal investigation had been launched by Nationwide and had identified five victims.

She said Kershaw, who also would drive a personalised BMW convertible, would process cash withdrawals from accounts but would pocket either some or all the money for herself.

Owen said Kershaw was interviewed by a financial investigator in November 2024, admitted what she had done and had been arrested by police.

Defence barrister Amy Edwards said Kershaw was suffering from a "compulsive spending addiction" at the time.

"She gave a full and frank admission to the offence and showed remorse to each of her victims. That is genuine remorse and regret for what she did," said Edwards.

Judge Petts said Kershaw needed to be jailed as a "deterrent" to other cashiers so as to "prevent others from doing the same".

He told her: "Your pattern of offending was repeated. You forged people's signatures or you would take their card to withdraw a large sum from the account and only hand over part of it.

"You were asked why you targeted those people in particular, you said they were 'easy targets who wouldn't notice the money going from their accounts.

"The reality is you only stopped stealing money because suspicions were raised about your lifestyle, investigations took place and your fraud was discovered."

articles.title: ‘Coordinate with Delhi Police’: Home secy directs states, UTs amid CJP mobilisation concerns ahead of banned protest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union home secretary Govind Mohan on Friday directed police chiefs of all states and Union territories to coordinate with the Delhi Police and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home secretary Govind Mohan on Friday directed police chiefs of all states and Union territories to coordinate with the Delhi Police and take preventive measures ahead of protests planned by youth pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in the capital, seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Mohan’s letter came after the Delhi Police denied permission to the CJP to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital. He cited concerns that the outfit and its supporters might attempt to enter Delhi despite the denial of permission.The letter described the proposed mobilisation as a “serious law-and-order concern”, citing intelligence inputs suggesting that the CJP and its supporters might attempt to enter Delhi from various states and Union territories despite the ban, potentially disrupting public peace and order.“To pre-empt any breach of public tranquility and to safeguard critical infrastructure, all States and UTs are hereby directed to coordinate with the Delhi Police and operationalise immediate preventive measures under the broad statutory and operational parameters, within the framework of the law,” the letter stated.It also called for continuous coordination among state and UT intelligence agencies, border transit authorities and the Delhi Police.“Continuous and real-time intelligence sharing must be maintained between State/UT intelligence agencies, border transit authorities, and the Delhi Police to ensure coordinated action,” it added.Mohan also cited what the letter described as the CJP’s “documented history of non-compliance with lawful directions” during past mobilisations, which resulted in disruptions to public order and damage to public and private property.The reference was to the July 20 clash between police and protesters who attempted to march to Parliament, demanding the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak issue. Pradhan resigned on July 25, bringing the agitation to an end.“Furthermore, the CJP and its supporting parties/organisations/individuals, during past events, have a documented history of non-compliance with lawful directions. Their past mobilisations from different states into Delhi have resulted in significant disruptions of public order and damage to public property/ Private property,” the letter stated.Emphasising the need for strict implementation of the directions, the letter described the maintenance of law and public order as a constitutional imperative.“The ministry (of home affairs) views the maintenance of law & order and public order as a non-negotiable constitutional imperative. Strict and uncompromising execution of the above is solicited to uphold the rule of law,” it added.Kumar has been at the centre of a controversy following a media report alleging a “rift” between him and the two Election Commissioners over several issues, including the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.The poll body subsequently maintained that differences of opinion were normal in a multi-member institution, adding that all decisions were ultimately taken unanimously.The Commission's decisions must either be unanimous or adopted by a 2:1 majority.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates.
